messages.author: b40b733c4b3d58f4
messages.subject: Two Questions
parts:
Dear Lavaan Experts:

I am revamping some of my notes for my forthcoming advanced SEM workshops with CARMA starting next week.  I’m mainly rerunning my examples using the latest lavaan version to see if there are any changes to the output from the last version that I used.  There was one change when reporting the fit indices that I would like to ask about.  Namely, the fit output has expanded the RMSEA.  For example, from one of my runs, I get:

Root Mean Square Error of Approximation:

 

  RMSEA                                                         0.024

  90 Percent confidence interval - lower         0.000

  90 Percent confidence interval - upper         0.070

  P-value H_0: RMSEA <= 0.050                    0.783

  P-value H_0: RMSEA >= 0.080                    0.017 

It’s the last line that is new to me.  If I were to use these values to address the fit of this model, what would I tell the participants?  In other words, how would you complete the following sentence. “According to the RMSEA, this is a well (or poor or mediocre) fitting model because . . . .”

I know that lavaan doesn’t yet have a routine that permits a random vector of slopes in multilevel structural equation models.  But my second question is, “is there perhaps a work around that allows one to do so by calling in some other package?”  There is strong interest among my participants to use slopes for hypotheses that include them.  

Thanks for your assistance as always.

Bob Vandenberg

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Two Questions
parts:
Bob--
     First question--That H0 p >= .08 looks like a test of not-close fit, going back to MacCallum, Browne & Sugawara (1996), though I think their default threshold was .05, not .08. The idea was to see if you had power to reject the hypothesis that the fit is bad. So if you did, then the model was "not bad." This way, you could use statistical power to your advantage, rather than just having it puff up minor discrepancy into a large chi-square.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Two Questions
parts:
Bob--
     For this one, I think a graph would be better. Your RMSEA = .025, then .05 and .08. You're on the left side of .05 so you fail to reject, and you're far enough away from .08 that you do reject.
     The problem with chi-square and the close-fit RMSEA is that a researcher who wants to protect their proposed model has an incentive to limit statistical power, using fewer, weaker indicators and limiting sample size. The test of not-close fit makes statistical power your friend and also, for people totally new to SEM, it reframes the test in terms of a conventional null hypothesis significance test, like for regression, where you want to reject the null. And yes, the other side, if you follow Meehl's "Physics vs Psychology" paper, is that the chi-square test structure is more similar to hypothesis testing in physics, where you specify a distribution based on theory and you try to conform to that distribution, and increasing power and precision make for an increasingly rigorous test.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Two Questions
parts:
Hello Bob,

As was already indicated by others, the last line in the RMSEA section
is the test of not-close fit. I only want to add that you can change the
default threshold(s) using the fm.args() argument in both the summary()
and fitMeasures() functions. See

?fitMeasures

As for the random slopes, a new package was is in the making that would
allow for this, but the main author left Academia, and the project is
now dead in the water. That is the less pleasant side of 'open-source'
software...

As for your second question, I usually refer to OpenMx. I also show
students the 'wide-format' trick, if only for didactical reasons
(because it is only useful for very small cluster sizes). See for example:

https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bmsp.12294?af=R

Yves.

Hi Yves,

I am interested in, as a user, fitting models with random slopes
in lavaan. Is the R package you mentioned one that works with lavaan?
Or is it a "standalone" package (depends on packages like lavaan
but use them behind the scene)? If it is open source and in GPL or a
similar license, and adopts a promising approach, maybe somebody
else can revive it? This practice is quite common in other areas with
open source free software as long as there is a demand, though not
so in R, it seems to me ... (perhaps I am wrong).

For the wide-format trick, the time difference you mentioned
between Mplus and lavaan is impressive. Perhaps user-friendly
functions for semTools can be written to generate lavaan syntax,
to make it easier for users to use the method in lavaan?

-- Shu Fai

parts:
On 6/11/23 12:56, Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝) wrote:
> I am interested in, as a user, fitting models with random slopes
> in lavaan. Is the R package you mentioned one that works with lavaan?

The code was based on these two papers:

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-020-09702-9
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-021-09770-5

both by Nicholas Rockwood (https://njrockwood.com/). For both papers, he
has written C++ code (often with an R interface), and the idea was to
generalize the code and create a C++ library, and then an R interface
(perhaps in a standalone package) that could be called from lavaan.

Code of the first paper is available here: https://osf.io/pxz5s/
Code of the second paper is available here: https://osf.io/w8u2q/

(I don't think the 'library code' was ever finished, let along published
on a public server)

Interfacing the C++ code of the two papers with lavaan is not trivial.
But if a volunteer wants to work on this, that would be great!

> For the wide-format trick, the time difference you mentioned
> between Mplus and lavaan is impressive. Perhaps user-friendly
> functions for semTools can be written to generate lavaan syntax,
> to make it easier for users to use the method in lavaan?

That is certainly possible. If only there was time (or again, a volunteer).

Yves.
